research.title: Read a study as a bounded answer
paragraphs: An empirical finding is attached to a market, sample, rule, implementation, and comparator. “Momentum has evidence” is too broad to tell you whether a long-only stock breakout with a two-day holding period deserves capital. Keep two separate questions in view: does past information change a return distribution, and can a specified investor exploit the change after costs and risk? The studies below deliberately include supportive, adverse, and narrower mechanistic results.

For each result, record what was ranked or measured, when it became observable, which position was held, and what was subtracted. Cross-sectional momentum compares stocks with other stocks. Time-series momentum compares an instrument with its own past. A stock/benchmark price ratio is a descriptive relative-performance series. RSI is an oscillator built from gains and losses. Sharing the word “strength” does not make these four objects equivalent.

When evidence disagrees, first compare the experiments. A monthly diversified winner-minus-loser portfolio and a daily index moving-average rule have different exposures and turnover. A mechanism in a dealer’s currency order book may motivate a stock-market hypothesis, but the transfer requires stock data. Treat an untested teaching rule as a disclosed illustration even when it resembles a researched family.

evidence.claim: The book’s toy rules are not independently validated strategies
evidence.location: This appendix and the Atlas-20 rule sheet
evidence.summary: Teaching rules are reproducible calculations and decisions; this edition does not report a held-out real-stock strategy trial.
evidence.limits: No claim of a profitable edge or recommended allocation.

research.title: Supportive stock evidence: cross-sectional momentum
paragraphs: Jegadeesh and Titman study NYSE/AMEX stocks during 1965–1989. They rank prior 3–12-month returns and form winner-minus-loser portfolios held over 3–12 months. These relative-return strategies earn positive average returns in that sample. The six-month formation/six-month holding analysis reports a 9.29% annual risk-adjusted return after an assumed 0.5% one-way transaction cost. The comparison concerns a portfolio spread and market/risk adjustments, not a promise that one rising stock keeps rising.

This is supportive evidence for a specified stock-momentum family. It does not establish the book’s candle thresholds, long-only implementation, or present-day net outcome. Short-side availability, financing, changing costs, different samples, and the chosen horizon matter. Follow the ranking convention and portfolio construction before borrowing the conclusion.

evidence.claim: A specified stock momentum portfolio showed positive historical returns
evidence.location: Sections I–IV; Table III and market-model/transaction-cost paragraph, printed pp. 67–78, especially p. 77 (PDF page 14).
evidence.summary: Read the universe, formation/holding rules, benchmarks, and assumed cost adjustment.
evidence.limits: Historical portfolio evidence; distinct from a discretionary breakout and not a current performance forecast.

study.rule: Equal-weight winner-minus-loser return deciles; rank prior 3–12 months; hold overlapping 3–12-month portfolios. Reported cost example: six/six months, without the one-week skip.
study.comparator: Winner-minus-loser spread and market-model risk adjustment; not a long-only stock account.
study.costs: Assumed 0.5% one-way cost, applied to observed turnover; no current retail cost estimate.
study.result: Positive sample returns; reported six/six-month risk-adjusted return after that cost: 9.29% annually.

research.title: Supportive evidence with a different market: time-series momentum
paragraphs: Moskowitz, Ooi and Pedersen examine 58 liquid futures/forward instruments across equity indexes, currencies, commodities and bonds. Their focused strategy uses the sign of each instrument’s past 12-month excess return, rebalances monthly, and scales positions by prior volatility. Over January 1985–December 2009, the diversified strategy outperforms a passive long comparison with similar ex ante volatility; the paper reports positive predictability across the instruments.

The figures label the instrument Sharpe ratios as gross. These are not net returns for a retail stock account, and futures/forward positioning is not ownership of individual common stocks. The useful inference is that own-return continuation has been observed under this specification. Stock selection, costs, roll conventions, leverage, and a different holding period must be studied separately.

evidence.claim: Time-series continuation has evidence in the studied futures/forward sample
evidence.location: Sections 2–4; equation (5), printed p. 236; Figure 2, p. 237 (PDF page 10); Figure 3 and Table 3.
evidence.summary: Checked market coverage, 12-month signal, volatility scaling, passive comparator, sample dates and gross-result label.
evidence.limits: No direct validation of individual-stock chart rules or the textbook’s execution model.

study.sample: 58 equity-index, currency, commodity and bond futures/forwards; main test January 1985–December 2009; instrument histories differ.
study.rule: Sign of own past 12-month excess return; monthly rebalance; prior-volatility scaling, 40% annual target per instrument, equal-weight aggregation.
study.comparator: Passive long in the same instruments with equal ex ante instrument risk; also factor-regression alphas.
study.costs: Figure 2 instrument Sharpe ratios are explicitly gross; do not interpret as retail net results.
study.result: Positive own-return predictability and diversified outperformance of the passive comparison in this sample.

research.title: Adverse evidence: rule selection and trading costs
paragraphs: Bajgrowicz and Scaillet test 7,846 technical rules on daily DJIA data from January 1897–July 2011 in the author-hosted version cited here. Their tests address the chance discoveries created by searching many rules, then examine whether past winners can be selected to perform later. Historical in-sample successes do not yield a reliable ex ante selection procedure in this experiment. Costs eliminate the out-of-sample performance of the investigated portfolios.

Table 5 reports break-even one-way costs rather than a universally correct fee. For the FDR-selected portfolios, the first three period ranges are 30–35, 0–5 and 0–5 basis points; the later periods have negative out-of-sample performance before costs. A basis point is 0.01 percentage point. The authors call these break-evens ex ante because costs are raised inside the selection procedure itself (pp. 22, 24), unlike break-evens computed after rules are chosen (p. 21). They are still backtest thresholds, not cost levels an investor would have measured beforehand. Compare turnover, spread and impact as well as commission. The study challenges extrapolating the best backtest; its daily index universe and tested rule set limit any claim about every stock method.

evidence.claim: Searching historical technical rules did not secure persistent net performance here
evidence.location: Author-hosted manuscript (sample ends July 2011): introduction p. 3; sections 4–5, pp. 20–25; Table 5, p. 49 (PDF page 49).
evidence.summary: Inspected false-discovery adjustment, chronological persistence tests and cost sensitivity against zero excess-performance criteria.
evidence.limits: Results concern the authors’ index/rule experiment; they neither prove all technical methods useless nor license ignoring adverse results.

study.sample: Daily DJIA index prices, January 1897–July 2011; author-hosted manuscript; the PDF text carries no version date.
study.rule: 7,846 technical rules; multiple-testing adjustment; ex ante rule portfolios updated monthly and evaluated in subsequent periods.
study.comparator: Zero excess-performance threshold and chronological persistence; Table 5 uses the Sharpe-ratio criterion.
study.costs: Table 5 FDR break-even one-way costs: 30–35, 0–5, 0–5 basis points in the first three periods; short lending costs treated separately.
study.result: Past winners cannot reliably be selected to persist; plausible costs erase remaining early-period out-of-sample gains; later FDR portfolios are negative before costs.

research.title: Mixed pattern evidence: information is not an executable profit
paragraphs: Lo, Mamaysky and Wang formalize ten chart-pattern classes with smoothing and recognition algorithms. Their 1962–1996 U.S. stock analysis compares returns conditional on detected patterns with unconditional distributions; some patterns add statistical information. The comparator is a distribution, not a completed net trading account. The paper’s detection and delay conventions matter because a visually obvious turning point may require subsequent observations.

A conditional distribution can differ without supplying a usable entry, stop, holding period or cost-adjusted advantage. This finding supports studying precisely defined patterns; it does not validate every hand-drawn shape or the book’s pattern practice rules. Recognition reproducibility and economic implementation are additional tests.

evidence.claim: Some algorithmically detected patterns contain incremental distributional information
evidence.location: Section II.A–B definitions/delay; Section III.B–F sample and results, Tables III–VIII; Section V conclusion, printed p. 1753. Tables I–II are pattern counts.
evidence.summary: Read the pattern definitions, sample conventions and conditional-versus-unconditional comparison.
evidence.limits: Not a demonstrated net-profit strategy and not evidence for arbitrary discretionary drawings.

study.sample: NYSE/AMEX and Nasdaq stock histories in 1962–1996; 50 randomly selected eligible stocks per market/five-year subperiod (10 per size quintile); at least 80% nonmissing daily prices.
study.rule: Kernel smoothing and ten algorithmically defined pattern classes; detection delay included before conditional next-day returns.
study.comparator: Pattern-conditioned versus unconditional return distributions, using goodness-of-fit tests.
study.costs: No completed net trading strategy or cost-adjusted account is tested by this distribution comparison.
study.result: Some defined patterns add distributional information; economic profit remains a separate question.

research.title: Mechanisms and behavior: useful explanations with limits
paragraphs: Osler studies nearly 9,700 conditional orders at one FX dealing bank during September 1999–April 2000 in dollar-yen, dollar-pound and euro-dollar. Requested execution prices cluster around round numbers, with different placement for take-profit and stop-loss orders. This supports an order-flow explanation for reactions and acceleration near levels. It is mechanism evidence in currency markets, not a cost-adjusted stock-rule trial.

Barber and Odean use account records for 66,465 common-stock households at one discount broker during 1991–1996; calculated returns run February 1991–January 1997. The most-active quintile earns an annualized geometric 11.4% net, the average household 16.4%, and the market 17.9%. Commissions and estimated spread separate net from gross results. Their method approximates trade timing and intramonth trading. Overconfidence is an explanation consistent with the observations, not an experimentally assigned cause.

Neither finding proves that a journal intervention improves returns or that a line on a stock chart reveals hidden stops. The book uses them to motivate explicit execution assumptions and disciplined process records. Whether those practices improve a particular reader’s decisions remains a separate empirical question.

evidence.claim: FX conditional orders cluster at round numbers
evidence.location: Introduction printed pp. 4–5; Section I.B (data), pp. 10–12; Section II.C (requested-rate distributions), pp. 14–15, Figures 1A–1B and 2A–2D; Section V conclusion.
evidence.summary: Inspected order sample, price-ending comparator and order-type differences; separate observation from the proposed price-response explanation.
evidence.limits: One bank and three currency pairs; no direct stock-level clustering or executable profit test.

study.sample: Almost 9,700 conditional orders at one FX dealing bank, September 1, 1999–April 11, 2000; dollar-yen, dollar-pound, euro-dollar.
study.rule: Compare requested execution-rate endings and stop-loss versus take-profit placement.
study.comparator: Observed price-ending frequencies versus a uniform distribution, and clustering across order types.
study.costs: No cost-adjusted stock strategy is tested; these are order-placement observations.
study.result: Execution rates cluster at round numbers; order types have different clustering. A bounded FX order-flow mechanism is proposed.

evidence.claim: Higher household turnover is associated with worse net performance here
evidence.location: Section II.A and footnote 4, printed pp. 777–778; Table I; Section II.B costs/timing; Figure 1 and Section IV/Table V, pp. 791–794.
evidence.summary: Inspected the common-stock sample, account/return date distinction, turnover groups, market comparator and gross/net calculation.
evidence.limits: One broker in one historical period; observational association does not establish motive or a journal intervention benefit.

study.sample: 66,465 common-stock households at one discount broker; account records January 1991–December 1996; measured returns February 1991–January 1997.
study.rule: Sort households by turnover; reconstruct monthly common-stock portfolio returns.
study.comparator: Turnover quintiles, average household and value-weighted market; risk-adjusted analyses also reported.
study.costs: Net returns subtract commissions and estimated bid–ask spread; main method approximates trade timing and omits intramonth round trips.
study.result: Annualized geometric net: most-active quintile 11.4%, average household 16.4%; market 17.9%. Overconfidence is an interpretation, not randomized causation.

research.title: Match confidence to the question being asked
paragraphs: Calculation certainty and investment confidence are different. A fully specified SMA can be verified exactly. Confidence in a future trading advantage needs a defined rule, comparable implementation, chronological evaluation and realistic costs. The comparison below describes this edition’s inspected evidence; “not tested here” is a boundary of this review, not a claim that no research exists.

Use the nearest study without changing its question. A pattern-distribution result cannot supply a net win rate. An FX order mechanism cannot reveal the stops in a stock. Positive monthly portfolio momentum and adverse daily index-rule selection can coexist because their markets, rules, holdings and comparisons differ. Before assigning capital, identify the missing experiment.

tables.title: What the inspected evidence establishes

evidence.claim: Evidence confidence depends on the question and implementation
evidence.location: This comparison table and the six original-study records above.
evidence.summary: Editorial synthesis keeps calculation support, historical empirical results, mechanisms and untested practices separate.
evidence.limits: Selected evidence audit, not an exhaustive or systematic literature review. No universal ranking of every technical method.

research.title: Trace glossary definitions to their support
paragraphs: A glossary entry is a compact definition, not a fresh investment claim. The groups below cover every term and abbreviation in this edition. Source-linked entries identify the actual defining passage; arithmetic entries point to a derivation; teaching-rule entries identify the book’s working vocabulary or local record convention. This classification does not mean every common term was invented here. It means no external authority or empirical benefit is being claimed for that wording.

Aliases inherit the full entry’s definition. For source-linked terminology, the cited provider or proponent establishes the convention, not trading effectiveness. Local thresholds, initialization, sampled endpoints, costs and recognition times remain part of the full chapter. Read those assumptions before using a short definition in isolation.

evidence.location: Chapter 1, A company and its quoted price; Fidelity What is technical analysis?, introduction and definition.
evidence.summary: Definition concerns market-generated prices/activity, compared with analysis of company value.
evidence.limits: Educational terminology does not establish effectiveness.

evidence.location: Chapter 2, Four numbers and one interval / Measure the candle one piece at a time; Fidelity What are charts?, Bar and Candlestick charts; StockCharts Introduction to Candlesticks, Formation.
evidence.summary: Checked four-price encoding, body and shadows; interval/session boundaries remain declared inputs.
evidence.limits: Color conventions differ; the geometry does not reveal intrabar order.

evidence.location: Chapter 3, What volume actually counts / Every transaction has two sides / Volume and liquidity; Fidelity Why to consider stock volume, Volume is vital; FINRA Understanding Market Liquidity and Your Investments, introduction.
evidence.summary: Volume counts transferred shares; liquidity also concerns price, available quantity and cost.
evidence.limits: This does not identify trader motives or promise an order fill.

evidence.limits: No distributions or intraday baselines should be silently assumed.

evidence.summary: Equal ratios have equal log spacing; prior prices are restated into consistent share units across a split.
evidence.limits: The regulator establishes share-unit mechanics; exact historical restatement is provider-specific, not licensed market data.

evidence.location: Chapter 5, Build the initial map / Draw one line; Fidelity Basic concepts of trend, 3 directions of trend and Trend lines.
evidence.summary: Definitions describe selected peaks/troughs and anchors; the chapter specifies its own swing detector.
evidence.limits: A line is an organizing convention, not proof of hidden demand or continued direction.

evidence.location: Chapter 5 Walk forward; Chapter 8 Double-top rule sheet; Chapter 9 Define failure without selecting the answer.
evidence.summary: Working definitions require a declared detector, transition/failure condition and observation time.
evidence.limits: Thresholds are local teaching choices, not a uniquely authoritative or empirically validated scanner.

evidence.summary: Paraphrased as observable reaction areas or conditional hypotheses. Breakout is a crossing of a predefined boundary.
evidence.limits: Price observations cannot identify hidden buyers/sellers or guarantee a future reaction; exact thresholds are local.

evidence.summary: Near-equal open/close defines doji; engulfing concerns the bodies rather than obligatory shadow coverage.
evidence.limits: Exact tolerances and confirmation choices are original, and no predictive performance is inferred.

evidence.location: Chapter 10 One line / Exponential weighting / The price of smoothing; Fidelity SMA/EMA and TradingView Moving Averages EMA Calculation.
evidence.summary: Arithmetic mean and recursive weighting distinguish the measures; abbreviations refer to the full entries. Retained history explains lag.
evidence.limits: Seed and multiplier must be specified; efficacy claims on provider pages are not adopted.

evidence.location: Chapter 10 Observe the first state; Chapter 11 A divergence is recognized after its selected peaks.
evidence.summary: Working vocabulary separates initialization history, ordering changes and matched extrema; precise rules control recognition time.
evidence.limits: Alternative seeds, ties and swing detectors can change readings/events.

evidence.location: Chapter 11 RSI compares / MACD asks; Fidelity ROC/RSI/MACD Calculation; TradingView RSI Calculation and How MACD is calculated.
evidence.summary: Checked percent ROC, smoothed gain/loss RSI, fast-minus-slow MACD and histogram difference; RSI alias uses the full entry.

evidence.summary: TR includes previous-close distances; ATR smooths range magnitude; bands use rolling SD around a mean.

evidence.summary: These working definitions identify preferential evidence selection, result-based grading and probability/frequency agreement.

sections.title: Historical case selection and data conventions
paragraphs: The historical cases below were selected to teach two data problems: an event-driven price move and a share-unit change. Selection is purposive, based on publicly documented episodes, rather than a random screen or an outcome-blind trading sample. Both the surge and subsequent fall in the selected GME episode are included. These cases cannot estimate a hit rate. Use the fictional cases earlier in the chapter to rehearse fully specified execution; these historical records teach what can and cannot be inferred from limited observations.

Provenance: GME, January 12–28, 2021, is reconstructed from SEC staff report section 3.2, printed pp. 18–19, published October 14, 2021. Prices use the dollar/share units reported for that period, not a later split-adjusted chart. Reported closing prices are distinguished from intraday highs; the report does not supply a complete OHLC series or exact timestamps for the highs. No dividend reinvestment or price adjustment is performed here. Two closes are derived from explicitly reported daily dollar changes, with the arithmetic disclosed in the table. Missing sessions remain missing.

Reuse basis: the SEC’s Webmaster FAQ states that Government-created site content is free to access and reuse, while some content such as stock art is excluded. This book attributes a few numeric facts from the staff report and makes its own table and diagram; it copies no vendor chart, artwork or logo. The FAQ is not a license for a vendor’s underlying market-data feed. The Apple case paraphrases the issuer’s dated announcement and uses original algebra, with no copied chart or photo.

sections.title: GME event reaction: a large move still leaves execution unknown
paragraphs: At the January 13 close, compare the two completed closing observations and volumes shown in the first panel. Price change is 31.40 − 19.95 = $11.45, or 57.39%; approximate share volume is roughly 20 times the previous session (about 144 million against 7 million shares). These are observations. The words “breakout” or “short squeeze” add an interpretation whose definition and evidence must be supplied.

Freeze a retrospective teaching decision at that close: require enough preceding OHLC to map and freeze a range boundary before January 13 (P1’s signal input), a defined event calendar, and an executable next-session opening offer before accepting P1’s long setup. The extracted report supplies none of those three inputs. The decision is “insufficient data; no modeled order.” January 27’s later price is hidden from this decision. A move eventually reaching a much higher price cannot repair missing information at the earlier cutoff.

sections.title: GME surge and reversal: do not turn a high into a closing fill
paragraphs: The second panel contains three consecutive closes. January 26 is $147.98, derived as $347.51 − $199.53; January 28 is $193.60, derived as $347.51 − $153.91. Close-to-close changes are +134.84% then −44.29%. The separately reported January 28 intraday high, $483, is not that day’s closing price.

At the January 27 close, a momentum description is supported by the supplied pair of closes. An execution claim is not: the next opening price, spread, halt timing, low, and fill sequence are absent. If a learner writes “bought the January 27 close and sold the January 28 high,” mark both fills as invented until independent transaction data supports them. The subsequent fall is a contrasting observation within the same chosen episode, not a countable failure of an unspecified strategy. Review outcome: the direction description transferred; the order model did not have enough input to run.

sections.title: Apple’s 2014 split: change the unit before classifying a break
paragraphs: Apple announced a seven-for-one stock split on April 23, 2014, with a June 2 record date and split-adjusted trading beginning June 9. This corporate-action case is selected to test unit consistency, independently of any later return. The announcement is usable as an event-calendar fact after its release; it supplies no entry or target prices.

At a June 6 analysis cutoff, the announced unit change belongs in the data plan for the next session. If a pre-split price is P and volume is V, a consistently split-adjusted comparison expresses that prior price as P/7 and prior share volume as 7V. A holder of N shares becomes a holder of 7N shares, so NP = (7N)(P/7) before other price movement. P, V and N are algebraic placeholders, not historical quotes. No dollar P&L is inferred. A raw discontinuity caused by the share unit is not evidence of a structural support failure.

Decision record: request a daily feed with its adjustment convention and the corporate-action flag before drawing a June 9 candle or computing a moving average across the date. The supplied announcement alone leads to a data-check decision, not a trade. This makes “skip” a completed analysis with a reason, rather than an empty chart opinion.

sections.title: A calendar-selected historical gallery: freeze the procedure first
paragraphs: The next gallery gives you a complete small OHLC window rather than a handful of famous-event facts. Before downloading prices, we fixed three symbols—Apple (AAPL), Microsoft (MSFT) and the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY)—and every month of 2016. The cutoff is the first available archive session on or after each month’s first day. Every one of the 36 symbol-month cells stays in the ledger. The symbols and year are teaching choices, not a historical investable universe; choosing familiar surviving securities introduces a selection limit even when dates are chosen without looking at their outcomes.

The exercise gate is deliberately simple: compare the cutoff close C with the arithmetic mean of the five preceding closes, excluding C. If C is not strictly higher, record “skipped.” If it is higher, observe the next five archive sessions against an upper level of 1.01C and a lower level of 0.99C. A session opening at or beyond a level resolves that side first. Otherwise compare its high and low: a sole upper touch is “favorable,” a sole lower touch “adverse,” and touching both in that first resolving bar is “ambiguous.” No touch within five sessions is “ordinary/unresolved.” These labels describe a price path under an invented exercise rule. They are not successful or failed historical trades.

The full ledger below contains 18 skips, six favorable paths, eleven adverse paths and one ordinary/unresolved path; none is an ambiguous first resolving bar. We show the earliest example of each represented class, with alphabetical symbol order breaking date ties. This representative choice is intentionally outcome-stratified, so the four illustrations are not a sample from which to estimate probabilities. Do not divide favorable counts by eligible counts to infer a strategy’s success rate. There is no order, position, fill, stop execution, cash account, commission model or held-out strategy test.

Provenance and reuse: Boris Marjanovic’s Huge Stock Market Dataset on Kaggle, version 3, provides the three daily files. Retrieved metadata explicitly declares CC0-1.0, and the depositor states that prices are adjusted for dividends and splits. We copied numeric observations into original tables and diagrams. The stated permission is the depositor’s; metadata does not identify an upstream provider or establish others’ rights. The local source snapshots, exact download URLs, SHA-256 hashes, extracts and frozen selection sheet are preserved in data/historical/ for independent inspection.

Data conventions: source date labels and all OHLC decimals are retained, in the archive’s adjusted dollar scale. Daily aggregation is reported, but exact regular/extended-session inclusion, time zone and adjustment formula are undocumented, and the adjustment vintage is bounded only by the depositor’s note “last updated 11/10/2017”. We therefore call them archive sessions, not certified regular-session candles. No missing date is interpolated. Volume is unused because its adjustment convention is unspecified. These are retrospectively adjusted records, not a reconstruction of prices published at each 2016 cutoff. The cutoff exercise hides future bars; it does not make the adjusted vintage contemporaneous. Before modeling real transactions, obtain documented raw quotes, corporate actions, precise sessions, spread and order information.

sections.title: AAPL January: a completed skip
paragraphs: At the January 4, 2016 cutoff, the preceding AAPL closes are 104.01, 102.83, 104.68, 103.32 and 101.35. Their sum is 516.19, giving a mean of 103.238. The cutoff close, 101.44, is below that mean, so the frozen exercise records a skip. January 4’s own low and high do not count as later level touches: the levels would only be frozen after this candle finishes.

Reveal January 5–11 only after recording the skip. The later decline is consistent with a weak path, but it was not needed to justify the gate decision. A reader who changes the cutoff or adds a short position after seeing the decline has written a different exercise. No skipped-window gain, avoided loss or fill is computed.

sections.title: MSFT February: the continuation check fails
paragraphs: At the February 1, 2016 MSFT cutoff, C = 52.347 exceeds the prior-five mean 50.1898. The gate permits observation; the frozen levels are 52.87047 above and 51.82353 below. This is a continuation hypothesis with a declared falsification check, not a forecast with a known probability.

The next archive session, February 2, opens at 51.830, narrowly inside the levels. Its low 50.377 crosses the lower level while its high 51.917 never reaches the upper one. The first resolving bar therefore classifies adverse. Nearest-cent rounding of 51.82353 gives 51.82: the open 51.830 is above both 51.82353 and 51.82, so the opening classification stays inside in this actual case. Preserve source precision through the comparison. For a separate fictional counterexample, a lower threshold 51.826 rounds to 51.83; an open 51.828 is above the exact threshold but at or below the rounded one. That named rounding policy would change inside to an opening lower-boundary touch. These fictional numbers do not replace the archived historical observations. The subsequent weakness cannot turn the hypothetical threshold into a real stop fill.

sections.title: AAPL March: favorable follow-through
paragraphs: At the March 1, 2016 AAPL cutoff, the preceding closes sum to 465.743 and average 93.1486. C = 97.309 passes the gate. The frozen lower/upper levels are 96.33591/98.28209. Write the observation and levels before reading the next five rows.

March 2’s entire range, 96.449–97.661, remains between the levels. On March 3, the open 97.357 is also inside, the low 97.232 remains above the lower level, and the high 98.459 exceeds the upper. This is favorable follow-through under the fixed path definition. March 4’s later high is irrelevant to the first-touch classification. Calling this a profitable trade would require entry timing, executable quotes, size and costs that the archive does not supply.

sections.title: SPY October: an ordinary unresolved window
paragraphs: At the October 3, 2016 SPY cutoff, C = 211.500 exceeds the prior-five mean 211.216. Its 209.385/213.615 levels are therefore observed over October 4–10. Across those five sessions, the lowest low is 209.750 and the highest high is 212.410. Both are inside the levels; no open can have crossed a level while lying within those recorded daily extremes.

The record ends ordinary/unresolved, even though individual closes move and the final close is slightly higher than the cutoff. A binary win/loss story would erase this case. Extending the horizon until something dramatic happens would revise the frozen observation window. The everyday lesson is that a completed analysis can reach its time limit without resolving the proposed interpretation.

sections.title: AAPL February: an ambiguous candle inside a skipped window
paragraphs: The fixed ledger has no ambiguous first resolving bar. We did not change its rule or add dates to manufacture one. After reviewing the cohort, we separately looked for a later candle whose open lies between the frozen levels while its high and low span both. The first such date is February 5 in the AAPL February window. This is a disclosed post-audit diagnostic, selected for its geometry; it does not replace that window’s skipped classification or establish an ambiguous trade.

At the February 1 cutoff, C = 92.839 is below the prior-five mean 93.2486, so the original gate skips. Its analytical levels, retained only for this diagnostic, are 91.91061 and 93.76739. Pose a fresh question after February 4 closes: what can the next daily candle tell us about the order in which those two levels are visited? No position is assumed to survive earlier bars, and neither later extreme is known at that question cutoff.

Reveal February 5: O/H/L/C = 93.429/93.816/90.690/91.009. The open is between the levels, high is above the upper, and low below the lower. Both high-before-low and low-before-high are compatible with these four observations. The alternative lines below are invented possible orders through the recorded extrema, not measured intraday paths or times. A target-first or stop-first assertion needs intraday observations and an execution model; a daily bar alone cannot settle it. Keep this ambiguity visible without undoing the original skip. One further caution concerns the data themselves. Apple’s $0.52 quarterly dividend was payable to holders of record on February 8, so under the 2016 settlement cycle the shares went ex-dividend on February 4, between the February 1 levels and this bar. The archive adjusts for dividends, so the levels and the bar carry different adjustment factors, and the high clears the adjusted upper level by only about $0.05, far less than the dividend. In unadjusted prices this bar probably reached only the lower level. The lesson concerns what any daily bar cannot reveal about order; it is not a claim that published February 5 prices spanned both levels.

sections.title: A price ratio is not a momentum portfolio
paragraphs: The relative index above describes one matched price comparison. Jegadeesh and Titman instead rank a stock universe, form winner-minus-loser portfolios and specify formation and holding periods; in their 1965–1989 NYSE/AMEX sample those portfolios earned positive returns. That portfolio evidence does not validate buying this example’s leader. The research appendix keeps its market, comparator and cost assumptions visible.

evidence.claim: Research boundary: a specified stock momentum portfolio showed positive historical returns
evidence.location: Sections I–IV; Table III and market-model/transaction-cost paragraph, printed pp. 67–78, especially p. 77 (PDF page 14).
evidence.summary: Read the universe, formation/holding rules, benchmarks, and assumed cost adjustment.
evidence.limits: Historical cross-sectional portfolio evidence; distinct from a single stock/benchmark price ratio and not a current performance forecast. The study also reports that part of the first-year abnormal return dissipates over the following two years.

study.rule: Rank prior 3–12-month returns; long winners, short losers; hold 3–12 months in overlapping portfolios. Cost example: six/six months.
study.comparator: Winner-minus-loser spread and market-model risk adjustment; not a long-only stock account.
study.costs: Assumed 0.5% one-way cost, applied to observed turnover; no current retail cost estimate.
study.result: Positive sample returns; reported six/six-month risk-adjusted return after that cost: 9.29% annually.

sections.title: Use the appropriate empirical comparator
paragraphs: For a rule-selection question, read the adverse DJIA study in the appendix, especially its chronological persistence and cost tests. For a pattern-information question, read Lo, Mamaysky and Wang’s distribution comparison. Neither supplies a performance estimate for Maya’s invented ledger. The study specification must match the claim.

sections.title: Do not confuse different evidence tests
paragraphs: A difference between conditional return distributions asks about information; a cost-adjusted portfolio return asks about implementation. The pattern and DJIA-rule studies in the Research and evidence appendix use different comparisons. Neither a statistically significant difference nor a gross mean alone supplies an executable net advantage.

sections.title: Ask what the evidence actually measured
paragraphs: Start with the evidence appendix when a claim sounds like “technical analysis works.” It compares a stock portfolio, a futures strategy, pattern-conditioned distributions and adverse rule-selection results. Ask which experiment would test the precise rule being proposed. A familiar chart label is not enough to identify it.

sections.title: A definition does not select a durable rule
paragraphs: Bajgrowicz and Scaillet’s DJIA experiment is relevant when a reader picks the best historical moving-average setting. Its adverse selection and cost findings concern a larger technical-rule family, not this exact SMA example. A crossover count is a path description; testing the rule still needs future evaluation and costs.

evidence.claim: Research boundary: searching historical technical rules did not secure persistent net performance here
evidence.location: Author-hosted manuscript (sample ends July 2011): introduction p. 3; sections 4–5, pp. 20–25; Table 5, p. 49 (PDF page 49).
evidence.summary: Inspected false-discovery adjustment, chronological persistence tests and cost sensitivity against zero excess-performance criteria.
evidence.limits: Results concern the authors’ index/rule experiment; they neither prove all technical methods useless nor license ignoring adverse results.

study.sample: Daily DJIA index prices, January 1897–July 2011; author-hosted manuscript; the PDF text carries no version date.
study.rule: 7,846 technical rules; multiple-testing adjustment; ex ante rule portfolios updated monthly and evaluated in subsequent periods.
study.comparator: Zero excess-performance threshold and chronological persistence; Table 5 uses the Sharpe-ratio criterion.
study.costs: Table 5 FDR break-even one-way costs: 30–35, 0–5, 0–5 basis points in the first three periods; short lending costs treated separately.
study.result: Past winners cannot reliably be selected to persist; plausible costs erase remaining early-period out-of-sample gains; later FDR portfolios are negative before costs.

sections.title: Three different momentum questions
paragraphs: RSI compares smoothed gains and losses inside one price series; MACD compares averages. Cross-sectional momentum ranks instruments against one another; time-series momentum uses each instrument’s own past return. The stock and futures studies in the appendix test the latter portfolio rules, not the RSI/MACD thresholds taught here.

evidence.claim: Research boundary: a specified stock momentum portfolio showed positive historical returns
evidence.location: Sections I–IV; Table III and market-model/transaction-cost paragraph, printed pp. 67–78, especially p. 77 (PDF page 14).
evidence.summary: Read the universe, formation/holding rules, benchmarks, and assumed cost adjustment.
evidence.limits: Historical portfolio evidence; distinct from a discretionary breakout and not a current performance forecast.

study.rule: Rank prior 3–12-month returns; long winners, short losers; hold 3–12 months in overlapping portfolios. Cost example: six/six months.
study.comparator: Winner-minus-loser spread and market-model risk adjustment; not a long-only stock account.
study.costs: Assumed 0.5% one-way cost, applied to observed turnover; no current retail cost estimate.
study.result: Positive sample returns; reported six/six-month risk-adjusted return after that cost: 9.29% annually.

evidence.claim: Research boundary: time-series continuation has evidence in the studied futures/forward sample
evidence.location: Sections 2–4; equation (5), printed p. 236; Figure 2, p. 237 (PDF page 10); Figure 3 and Table 3.
evidence.summary: Checked market coverage, 12-month signal, volatility scaling, passive comparator, sample dates and gross-result label.
evidence.limits: No direct validation of individual-stock chart rules or the textbook’s execution model.

study.sample: 58 equity-index, currency, commodity and bond futures/forwards; main test January 1985–December 2009; instrument histories differ.
study.rule: Sign of own past 12-month excess return; monthly rebalance; prior-volatility scaling, 40% annual target per instrument, equal-weight aggregation.
study.comparator: Passive long in the same instruments with equal ex ante instrument risk; also factor-regression alphas.
study.costs: Figure 2 instrument Sharpe ratios are explicitly gross; do not interpret as retail net results.
study.result: Positive own-return predictability and diversified outperformance of the passive comparison in this sample.

sections.title: A plausible mechanism has a market boundary
paragraphs: Osler’s order data provide a concrete example of round-number clustering in currency markets. They do not reveal the orders near Harbor’s fictional zone or test a stock support rule. Keep the mechanism as a hypothesis until the relevant stock data and executable rule have been evaluated.

evidence.claim: Research boundary: FX conditional orders cluster at round numbers
evidence.location: Introduction printed pp. 4–5; Section I.B (data), pp. 10–12; Section II.C (requested-rate distributions), pp. 14–15, Figures 1A–1B and 2A–2D; Section V conclusion.
evidence.summary: Inspected order sample, price-ending comparator and order-type differences; separate observation from the proposed price-response explanation.
evidence.limits: One bank and three currency pairs; no direct stock-level clustering or executable profit test.

study.sample: Almost 9,700 conditional orders at one FX dealing bank, September 1, 1999–April 11, 2000; dollar-yen, dollar-pound, euro-dollar.
study.rule: Compare requested execution-rate endings and stop-loss versus take-profit placement.
study.comparator: Observed price-ending frequencies versus a uniform distribution, and clustering across order types.
study.costs: No cost-adjusted stock strategy is tested; these are order-placement observations.
study.result: Execution rates cluster at round numbers; order types have different clustering. A bounded FX order-flow mechanism is proposed.

sections.title: Observation does not prove an intervention
paragraphs: Barber and Odean’s brokerage sample connects turnover with net performance after trading costs. It does not assign people to journal, pause or counterargument exercises. The process proposals in this chapter aim to make decisions inspectable; this edition supplies no experiment showing that they improve returns.

evidence.claim: Research boundary: higher household turnover is associated with worse net performance here
evidence.location: Section II.A and footnote 4, printed pp. 777–778; Table I; Section II.B costs/timing; Figure 1 and Section IV/Table V, pp. 791–794.
evidence.summary: Inspected the common-stock sample, account/return date distinction, turnover groups, market comparator and gross/net calculation.
evidence.limits: One broker in one historical period; observational association does not establish motive or a journal intervention benefit.

study.sample: 66,465 common-stock households at one discount broker; account records January 1991–December 1996; measured returns February 1991–January 1997.
study.rule: Sort households by turnover; reconstruct monthly common-stock portfolio returns.
study.comparator: Turnover quintiles, average household and value-weighted market; risk-adjusted analyses also reported.
study.costs: Net returns subtract commissions and estimated bid–ask spread; main method approximates trade timing and omits intramonth round trips.
study.result: Annualized geometric net: most-active quintile 11.4%, average household 16.4%; market 17.9%. Overconfidence is an interpretation, not randomized causation.

sections.title: What the journal cannot certify
paragraphs: A timestamped journal makes the author’s stated plan and later edits visible. It cannot by itself establish calibration, causation or a profitable strategy. Keep every eligible opportunity and use the testing chapter’s chronology before treating a journal’s selected wins as evidence.

sections.title: Atlas-20 still needs its own empirical test
paragraphs: The research appendix gives supportive momentum evidence and adverse rule-selection evidence under other specifications. Atlas-20’s thresholds, allocation and fills are original teaching choices. The cash reconciliation proves that the scenario’s accounting works; it is not a held-out real-stock trial or an estimate of its profitability.
